title: Reading real Irish
goal: Read texts, songs, and blessings in real Irish — all with what you've gained from the twenty units you've finished.
bekal: read a short Irish text without a dictionary
understand the chorus of the most often sung folk song
use the blessings and greetings native speakers use

dialogs.title: Comhrá — An rang deireanach
dialogs.intro: The last class before the holidays. Aoife gives Budi a few things to read on his own.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Sin é an cúrsa críochnaithe. Comhghairdeas, a Bhudi!
lines.id: The course is over. Congratulations, Budi!
lines.literal: there the course finished. congratulations, O Budi!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Go raibh míle maith agat. Ach níl mo chuid Gaeilge foirfe fós.
lines.id: Thanks a lot. But my Irish isn't perfect yet.
lines.literal: may-be thousand good at-you. but not-is my portion Irish perfect yet.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Ní bheidh sí foirfe go deo — agus ní gá di a bheith.
lines.id: It will never be perfect — and it doesn't need to be.
lines.literal: not will-be it perfect till ever — and not need to-it to be.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Seo leabhar beag duit. Agus amhrán — is é an ceann is cáiliúla ar fad.
lines.id: Here's a little book for you. And a song — the most famous one of all.
lines.literal: here book small to-you. and song — is it the one is most-famous on length.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Níl. Tuigfidh tú beagnach gach focal ann.
lines.id: No. You'll understand almost every word.
lines.literal: not-is. will-understand you almost every word in-it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Agus na comharthaí ar an mbóthar — tuigim iad anois freisin.
lines.id: And the signs on the street — I understand them now too.
lines.literal: and the signs on the street — understand-I them now too.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Sin é an rud is tábhachtaí. Tosaigh ag léamh, agus ná stop.
lines.id: That's the most important thing. Start reading, and don't stop.
lines.literal: there the thing is most-important. start at reading, and don't stop.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rachaidh mé go dtí an Ghaeltacht arís an bhliain seo chugainn.
lines.id: Next year I'll go to the Gaeltacht again.
lines.literal: will-go I to the Gaeltacht again the year this toward-us.

lines.speaker: Aoife:
lines.text: Go n-éirí an bóthar leat. Agus labhair Gaeilge le gach duine!
lines.id: Good luck on the road. And speak Irish with everyone!
lines.literal: may rise the road with-you. and speak Irish with every person!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Labhróidh. Slán, a Aoife — agus go raibh maith agat as gach rud.
lines.id: I will. Bye, Aoife — and thanks for everything.
lines.literal: will-speak. safe, O Aoife — and may-be good at-you for every thing.

notes: **Mo chuid Gaeilge — "my portion of Irish".** For things you can't count — language, money, hair, time — Irish puts the word *cuid* ("portion") after the possessive: *mo chuid airgid* (my money), *do chuid gruaige* (your hair), *a chuid ama* (his time). Without *cuid*, the sentence sounds as if you owned all the Irish in the world.
**Go deo, go brách — "forever".** Used in a negative sentence to mean "never": *Ní bheidh sí foirfe go deo*. You'll often see *go brách* on banners and in songs — *Éire go brách*, "Ireland forever".

**Is é an ceann is cáiliúla — the superlative.** *Is* + the comparative form means "most": *is fearr* (best), *is mó* (biggest), *is tábhachtaí* (most important), *is cáiliúla* (most famous). The form is exactly the one used after *níos* for "more" — only the word in front changes.

**Go n-éirí an bóthar leat.** Literally "may the road rise with you" — Ireland's best-known travel blessing, which circulates in English as *May the road rise to meet you*. Note the *n-* slipped in before *éirí*: that's urú after *go*, just as you learned in Unit 19.

blocks.text: The text below is written only with words and forms from these twenty units. Read it first without looking at the translation; check afterwards.

blocks.title: Bliain i nGaillimh
items: Is mise Budi. Is as an Indinéis mé, ach tá mé i mo chónaí i nGaillimh anois. Tá mé ag foghlaim Gaeilge le bliain amháin.
Éirím ar a seacht gach maidin. Ólaim tae agus ithim arán. Ansin siúlaim chuig an scoil. Tosaíonn an rang ar a naoi.
Tá mo mhúinteoir go hiontach. Aoife is ainm di. Labhraíonn sí go mall liom, agus tuigim beagnach gach rud anois.
Tar éis an ranga, téim go dtí an chathair. Uaireanta ceannaím leabhar, uaireanta ólaim caife le mo chairde. Is breá liom an chathair seo.
Dé Sathairn seo caite chuaigh mé go Conamara. Bhí an aimsir go dona ar maidin, ach ghlan sé tráthnóna. Chonaic mé an fharraige agus na sléibhte. Bhí sé ar fheabhas.
Rachaidh mé abhaile sa samhradh, ach fillfidh mé i mí Mheán Fómhair. Tá a fhios agam anois: ní bheidh mé réidh go deo, ach tá mé ag foghlaim. Agus is fearr Gaeilge bhriste ná Béarla cliste.

blocks.text: I'm Budi. I'm from Indonesia, but I live in Galway now. I've been learning Irish for a year. — I get up at seven every morning. I drink tea and eat bread. Then I walk to school. The class starts at nine. — My teacher is wonderful. Her name is Aoife. She speaks slowly to me, and now I understand almost everything. — After class, I go into town. Sometimes I buy a book, sometimes I have coffee with my friends. I love this city. — Last Saturday I went to Conamara. The weather was bad in the morning, but it cleared up in the afternoon. I saw the sea and the mountains. It was amazing. — I'll go home in the summer, but I'll come back in September. I know now: I'll never be perfect, but I'm learning. And broken Irish is better than clever English.
The folk song Irish people sing most, and the one you'll hear most often in a pub. Its chorus is just four lines, and three of them are the same.

blocks.title: An curfá — the chorus
items: Óró, sé do bheatha 'bhaile,
Óró, sé do bheatha 'bhaile,
Óró, sé do bheatha 'bhaile,
Anois ar theacht an tsamhraidh.

blocks.text: So the whole chorus means: **"Welcome home, now that summer is coming."** The phrase *sé do bheatha* literally means "it is your life" and is an old way of saying welcome — its plural is *sé bhur mbeatha*. The word *'bhaile* is *abhaile* ("home, homeward") with its a clipped off to fit the rhythm.

blocks.title: If you want to sing it
items: The song has two lives: originally a song welcoming a bride, then in the early twentieth century Pádraig Mac Piarais wrote new verses that turned it into a song of the independence struggle.
What people sing in the pub is almost always just the chorus above, so these four lines are enough to join in.
The easiest recordings to find: the version by The Dubliners and the one by Sinéad O'Connor. Listen while following the words — it's the most enjoyable way to train your ear.

blocks.text: Irish is very rich in short blessings, and most of them are used every day as ordinary greetings. They all start with *go*, meaning "may" — which, as you know from Unit 19, brings urú.

blocks.title: And one last blessing from this book
items: *Go n-éirí an bóthar leat, agus go raibh an ghaoth i gcónaí ar do chúl.*
"May the road rise with you, and may the wind always be at your back."

You can now take the whole sentence apart yourself: *go* + urú, *an bóthar* with the article, *leat* the *le* form, *go raibh* the wishing form (foshuiteach) of *bí* after *go* — not the past, *an ghaoth* with séimhiú because *gaoth* is feminine, *i gcónaí* with urú after *i*, and *do chúl* with séimhiú because of *do*.
Seven rules in one blessing — and you understand all seven. *Maith thú!*

exercises.prompt: Take apart the blessing *Go n-éirí an bóthar leat*. Answer in English.
items: Why is there an *n-* before *éirí*?
What is the base word of *leat*?
What does *an bóthar* mean?
What does *go* at the start of the sentence mean here?
What is the literal translation of the whole sentence?
When is this sentence used?

answers: Is as an Indinéis é. — Tá sé ina chónaí i nGaillimh. — Éiríonn sé ar a seacht. — Aoife is ainm di. — Chuaigh sé go Conamara. — Fillfidh sé i mí Mheán Fómhair.
an exclamation with no meaning, like "oh!" — welcome (literally "it is your life") — home, homeward — now — at the coming — summer
Go n-éirí an bóthar leat. — Go raibh maith agat. — Bíodh biseach ort. — Codladh sámh. — Sláinte mhaith! — Lá breithe sona duit.

Because *go* brings urú, and a word starting with a vowel gets *n-*. — Its base word is *le*, meaning "with". — "The road": *bóthar* with the article *an*. — *Go* here means "may". — "May rise the road with you." — When seeing off someone who's leaving, like "have a safe trip" or "good luck".
